Project Mode.Purpose: A project tracks the pipeline runs of one compartment. It fills the input files of the stages for you. A project has one baseline, zero or more scans and zero or more diffs.
Project Mode.Baseline: The first scan of the compartment. Stages 1 to 4 (SLAM, Level, Cleanup, Segment) run once for the baseline. Stage 4 is optional.
Project Mode.Scans: Later scans of the same compartment, to check for new damage. Each scan runs its own Stages 1 to 4. Push 'New Scan' to add a scan. Each scan needs its own raw source file.
Project Mode.Diffs: A diff compares two scans. Stages 5 to 8 (Diff, Classify, Surface, Export) run for each diff. A diff can compare a scan with the baseline or with an earlier scan. For each side, Stage 5 uses the Stage 4 output if Stage 4 ran, and the Stage 3 output if not. If Stage 4 also wrote the copy without the points outside the room (<name>_envelope_filtered.ply), the diff uses that copy. Push 'New Diff' to add a diff.
Project Mode.Pipeline selectors: Two lists at the top of the main window select the pipeline for the stage buttons. 'Source pipeline' selects the baseline or a scan, for Stages 1 to 4. 'Diff pipeline' selects a diff, for Stages 5 to 8. The status label shows the next stage of each selected pipeline.
Project Mode.Manual mode: Each stage also works without a project. Select the input files with Browse, or tick 'Use manual file selection instead' in the dialog. In manual mode, no project.json file is written.
Project Mode.Help buttons: The '?' button at the end of a field row opens a short explanation. It tells what the field does, what a smaller or larger value does, and when to change it. Click anywhere else to close it.

Units.Centimetres: Small length values show in centimetres (cm). Examples are voxel sizes, distance thresholds, cluster gap tolerances, M3C2 scales, the registration RMS, the Stage 7 recipe values and the damage detail radius. Each of these fields has (cm) in its label.
Units.Metres: Range values show in metres (m). These are the min range override and the map max range in Stage 1. Each of these fields has (m) in its label.
Units.Files: The scripts, the KISS-ICP configuration file, project.json, the M3C2 parameter file, CloudCompare and the USD files all use metres. The application changes centimetres to metres before it starts a script. Do not change the values in these files to centimetres.
Units.Check: Before a run, the application examines each centimetre value. If a value is very small or very large, the application asks you to confirm it. A frequent cause is a metre value in a centimetre field. For example, 0.05 in a centimetre field is 0.5 mm, not 5 cm.

Stage 1: SLAM.Purpose: Builds a 3D point cloud map from a raw lidar recording, and finds the path of the sensor. There are two backends. KISS-ICP reads PointCloud2 topics from a rosbag (Ouster or Hesai driver). Ouster CLI reads raw Ouster packets directly.
Stage 1: SLAM.Inputs:
- Backend: KISS-ICP or Ouster CLI.
- Source: a .pcap, .osf or ROS1 .bag file, or a ROS2 bag folder (a .db3 file and metadata.yaml). Both backends detect the type. In project mode, the box fills from the raw source of the selected pipeline.
- Output .ply.
- Ouster CLI: Meta JSON file (necessary for a .pcap), voxel size, map max range, visualizer.
- KISS-ICP: sensor preset, config .yaml, voxel size override, range limits, dataloader and topic, flying-pixel filter (in Advanced).
Stage 1: SLAM.Outputs: One .ply map. In project mode, the result is recorded on the selected pipeline (the baseline or the scan).
Stage 1: SLAM.What to expect:
The run time depends on the length of the recording. The orientation of the map is arbitrary. Neither backend levels the map, so it keeps the tilt that the sensor had at the first frame. Stage 2 (Level) corrects it.

KISS-ICP config: without a config file, KISS-ICP uses defaults for an outdoor vehicle (max_range 100 m). In a compartment, the map then has far fewer points. The Config field holds the bundled kiss_icp_config_indoor.yaml. Make sure that it is not a different file with the same name, for example the metadata.yaml of a ROS bag. For a Hesai sensor, select the Hesai preset in 'Sensor preset'.

Min range override: a sensor on a robot can see part of its own mount. These points are at the same place in each frame. They form a dense blob near the sensor in the map. The SLAM solver can align each frame to the blob and not to the room. The result is a noisy map or a map with a wrong shape. The override removes the points that are closer than the set distance, before SLAM runs. Start with 0.2 to 0.3 m. A value that is too high also removes real details near the sensor. The label 'This config's own min_range' shows the value of the config file.

Raw packets: some recordings hold raw Ouster packets and no PointCloud2 topic. KISS-ICP cannot read raw packets. When you select a ROS2 bag folder, Stage 1 reads its metadata.yaml. If it finds raw packets and no PointCloud2 topic, it asks if you want to convert the bag with decode_raw_packets.py. This is the same for both backends. Ouster CLI reads raw packets directly, but a decoded copy is also useful. After the conversion, the decoded bag becomes the input of the pipeline in project mode, or fills Source in manual mode. The button 'Check Source for Raw Packets...' does the same check for a path that you typed.

Map limits: 'Map max range' removes far noise, for example in open areas. The saved map does not include points that are farther than this distance from the sensor. With Ouster CLI, SLAM registration still uses the full sensor range. With KISS-ICP, the value replaces the max_range of the config for this run. Both backends show the same value in their own section, so the value stays when you change the backend. Do not lower max_range in the config file for this purpose. KISS-ICP then also removes far points from its own map. The saved map then keeps only the area near the last robot position.

Map max horizontal distance and map max vertical distance (KISS-ICP only): these limits work in two directions. The horizontal distance is along the floor. The vertical distance is up or down from the sensor. 'Vertical' is the up direction of the sensor at the start of the scan. Use a horizontal limit to remove far noise in an open area and keep a high ceiling. A point must be inside all the limits that you set, also 'Map max range'.
Stage 1: SLAM.Next steps: Open the map in CloudCompare to check it. Then use it as the input of Stage 2 (Level). To compare the two backends, give both the same source and different output names.

Stage 2: Level.Purpose: Corrects the tilt of the SLAM map. It finds the floor plane with RANSAC. Then it turns the cloud so that the floor is horizontal at Z = 0.
Stage 2: Level.Inputs:
- Raw SLAM output .ply (fills from Stage 1 in project mode).
- Output .ply.
- Distance threshold, max planes to search, min plane size, horizontal threshold: the RANSAC settings.
- Remove stray points far below the floor (Advanced, off by default).
- 'Skip Level' (project mode only).
Stage 2: Level.Outputs: A leveled .ply. The floor plane is horizontal and at Z = 0.
Stage 2: Level.What to expect:
The tool output lists each candidate plane, its height (Z) and if it passes the horizontal threshold. Level picks the LOWEST candidate that passes, not the biggest one. A ceiling can have more points than a floor, because it has less clutter. If the floor has very few points, or the output shows a low-horizontality warning or a fallback warning, check the result in CloudCompare before you use it.

Stray points below the floor: ghost returns under the floor can go into Stage 5 and show as damage. The option removes the small groups of points that are far below the local floor. The tool output always counts these points.

Skip Level: the button records Stage 2 as done, with the Stage 1 file as its output. Use it for a cloud that is already level, or for a baseline and a scan that are already registered to each other. Level turns each cloud on its own floor, and two different turns break the registration. To undo, run Stage 2.
Stage 2: Level.Next steps: Open the leveled cloud in CloudCompare and check that the floor is horizontal. Then use it as the input of Stage 3 (Cleanup).

Stage 3: Cleanup.Purpose: Removes noise points from the SLAM map with Statistical Outlier Removal (SOR). It can also align the cloud to a baseline map with ICP, to correct the remaining drift.
Stage 3: Cleanup.Inputs:
- Input .ply (fills from Stage 2 in project mode).
- SOR neighbors and SOR std dev (Advanced).
- Optional: Align to (a baseline .ply). In project mode, for a scan, the button 'Use Project Baseline' fills the box with the Cleanup output of the baseline. This is the usual choice. In manual mode, use the registered-baseline list.
- Optional: ICP final overlap in percent (10 to 100, only with a baseline).
- Output .ply.
- Optional: register the output as a manual-mode baseline (Advanced).
Stage 3: Cleanup.Outputs: A cleaned .ply at the path that you selected. If the alignment ran, CloudCompare also saves a copy of the baseline in the same folder (a CloudCompare limit). It also saves a registration log .txt. The log has the RMS, the transformation matrix and the point counts. In project mode, the RMS and the path of the log are recorded on the Cleanup stage of the pipeline.
Stage 3: Cleanup.What to expect:
CloudCompare names the output file itself. Stage 3 finds the new .ply and renames it to the path that you selected.

A manual-mode baseline and the baseline of a project are two different things. The baseline of a project is recorded in project.json. You do not register it. The registry (baseline_registry.json) is a separate list that you use only when no project is open.

The ICP RMS is the nearest-point distance after the alignment. It can be much larger than the misalignment that M3C2 sees along the surface. 'ICP final overlap' (for example 90) leaves out the points that match worst. It lowers the RMS only if some points match badly. The report names the overlap that Stage 3 used. For the Registration RMS of Stage 5, use the estimate in the Stage 5 report, which comes from the M3C2 distances.
Stage 3: Cleanup.Next steps: Open the cleaned .ply in CloudCompare and check the alignment. A lower RMS in the registration log is better. If this output is the baseline of the compartment, there is nothing to align it to. The baseline pipeline of the project is the record, and no other step is necessary.

Stage 4: Segment (optional).Purpose:
Optional stage. You can go from Stage 3 (Cleanup) directly to Stage 5 (Diff). Stage 5 then uses the Stage 3 output. Without Stage 4, the points outside the room stay in the data, and Stage 8 cannot show surface names on the damage sites.

Stage 4 divides a cleaned cloud into floor, ceiling, single walls and unclassified points. It uses segment_planes.py, which finds planes in the same way as Stage 2 and keeps all surfaces. It runs once for each baseline or scan, after Cleanup. It does not run for each diff.
Stage 4: Segment (optional).Inputs:
- Cleaned .ply, best leveled first (fills from Stage 3 in project mode).
- Output folder (not one file).
- Distance threshold, max planes, min plane size, horizontal threshold, max horizontal Z span: the plane settings.
- Cluster filter and its gap tolerance and minimum points (on by default).
- Merge of split planes and its normal similarity and distance (on by default).
- Option: write each surface as its own .ply (off by default).
- Option: flag unclassified points outside the room as junk, its margin, and a separate copy without these points (all on by default).
Stage 4: Segment (optional).Outputs:
Stage 4 writes into one folder. '<name>' is the name of the output folder, so the files of different runs stay different when you open them outside their folder.
- <name>_classified.ply: every input point, with the fields 'classification' (the surface), 'is_envelope' and 'outside_envelope'. The project records this file as the output of the stage.
- <name>_envelope.ply: only the classified surfaces, without clutter. It is a good input for Stage 7.
- <name>_envelope_filtered.ply: the classified cloud without the junk points. Stage 5 uses this copy. If no point is outside the room, the copy is not written.
- manifest.json: the list of the surfaces.
With the option for separate surfaces, Stage 4 also writes <name>_floor.ply, <name>_ceiling.ply, <name>_wall_1.ply and so on, and <name>_unclassified.ply. In project mode, the surface list and the results of the outside filter are recorded on the Segment stage of the pipeline.
Stage 4: Segment (optional).What to expect:
The classification of floor, ceiling and walls uses height and direction. If the surface list in the run report shows a wall as ceiling, or the reverse, check the settings. If a wall is missing, turn on the separate surfaces and run again. Then look at <name>_unclassified.ply. A flat group of points there is usually the missing wall, broken up by clutter. You can also look at the field 'classification' in <name>_classified.ply (0 = unclassified).

Outside filter: the floor, ceiling and wall points show the footprint and the height of the room. Stage 4 checks each unclassified point against them, with some margin. A point outside both is probably junk, such as scan noise from beyond the walls. It gets 'outside_envelope' = 1. Stage 4 does not remove any point from <name>_classified.ply. The field is a label. Raise the margin if real clutter near a wall is flagged. Lower it if junk near a wall is not flagged. If the report says that the filter did not run, Stage 4 did not find enough floor, ceiling and wall surface to find the footprint of the room. Check the surface list first.
Stage 4: Segment (optional).Next steps: Open <name>_classified.ply in CloudCompare and colour it by 'classification'. Colour it by 'outside_envelope' to check the flags. If real content is flagged, raise the margin and run again. Use <name>_envelope.ply as the input of Stage 7 (Surface) to get one shell for the floor, ceiling and walls together.

Stage 5: Diff (M3C2).Purpose: Uses M3C2 (multiscale model-to-model cloud comparison) to measure the distance between two clouds at each point. It shows where the compartment changed between a reference scan and a comparison scan.
Stage 5: Diff (M3C2).Inputs:
- Baseline .ply and Comparison .ply. In project mode, they fill from the 'reference' and 'comparison' of the selected diff. The reference is the baseline or an earlier scan. The comparison is always a scan. In manual mode, use Browse and the registered-baseline list.
- For a Stage 4 (Segment) output, use the file with the note 'outside-room points removed' (<name>_envelope_filtered.ply). It does not have the scan noise and the returns from beyond the walls, which can show as false damage. If you select <name>_classified.ply and the copy exists, Run asks which file to use. Push Yes to use the copy.
- Normal scale, Search scale and Search depth ('Check Point Spacing' fills them).
- Registration RMS (fills from Stage 3 in project mode; or use 'Load from Stage 3' or 'Check Registration (quick)...').
- M3C2 params file (.txt): make it with 'Generate Params File...', or select a file that you made in CloudCompare (Plugins > M3C2 Distance).
Stage 5: Diff (M3C2).Outputs: Several .ply files. CloudCompare saves each cloud that it loaded, not only the M3C2 result. The result is the file with an M3C2 distance field. It is usually the sparser cloud. The other files are unchanged copies of the inputs. This is a limit of CloudCompare. In project mode, Stage 5 finds the result file and records it on the diff stage. It also records the params file, the registration error and the two input files (reference_input and comparison_input). Stage 8 uses reference_input to put surface names on the damage sites.
Stage 5: Diff (M3C2).What to expect:
A run report shows after each successful run. It names the output files. It also shows for each input if the points outside the room were removed.

Params file: 'Generate Params File...' writes the four values of this page (normal scale, search scale, search depth, registration error) and copies all other values from a reference file. A params file does not change when you change a value. Push 'Generate Params File...' again after each change. Set Search scale and Search depth in proportion to Normal scale. The 'Guess params' function of CloudCompare does not do this automatically. A wrong Search scale gives round edges.

Quick registration check: push 'Check Registration (quick)...' to estimate the Registration RMS before you run Stage 5. Fill Normal scale, Search scale and Search depth first. The check takes a random sample of the baseline points and measures the distance along the surface normal to the comparison. It takes 5 to 30 seconds. It does not use CloudCompare, so the result is an estimate. Push Yes to put the value in the Registration RMS field. Then make the params file again. The check needs numpy, scipy and plyfile.

Registration check in the report: the report starts with the REGISTRATION CHECK. Its first line says what to do, for example 'CHANGE THE REGISTRATION RMS FROM 5.39 cm TO 0.31 cm AND RUN AGAIN'. After the run, the check reads the M3C2 distances. It gives the offset between the scans (median), the spread of the distances (1.4826 x the median absolute deviation) and the 95 % value. If the Registration RMS that you entered is much larger than the spread, the report gives the spread as a value to try. If more than 2 % of the distances are far from the median, the report gives this share. The spread does not describe these points, so look at them in CloudCompare. The spread includes some surface roughness, so it is an upper estimate of the registration error. The check needs numpy and plyfile.
Stage 5: Diff (M3C2).Next steps: Open the result cloud in CloudCompare and set the active scalar field to 'M3C2 distance'. Check the colour scale (red = positive change, blue = negative change). Then use the result as the input of Stage 6 (Classify).

Stage 6: Classify.Purpose: Finds the real damage in the M3C2 result. It flags the points that moved more than their uncertainty and more than the distance threshold. It then groups the flagged points into damage sites, so that a single flagged point with no neighbours is not damage.
Stage 6: Classify.Inputs:
- M3C2 diff result .ply (fills from Stage 5 in project mode). It must have the M3C2 distance field.
- Distance threshold. 'Check Threshold Against the Diff File...' and 'Load RMS & Suggest Threshold' help to find a value.
- Registration error in the uncertainty: measure it from the distances, or keep the value of Stage 5.
- Clustering (on by default): the cluster method, gap tolerance, density and minimum site size. The option 'auto' sets these from the point spacing.
- Keep all points (on by default): the output keeps every point and adds flag fields, so that Stage 7 can make a full surface.
- Find holes (on by default): finds holes, added material and removed material. It needs clustering.
- Limits for the size and the shape of the sites (main block).
- Removal of the smooth background (Advanced).
- Option: a second M3C2 result with another scale, to keep only the sites that both runs find (Advanced).
Stage 6: Classify.Outputs:
A .ply file. With 'Keep all points' on, it has every point, a field 'classified' (1 = above the threshold) and a field 'cluster_id' (the damage site, -1 = none). With 'Keep all points' off, it has only the flagged points. With clustering on, Classify also saves a '.clusters.json' file. It lists, for each damage site, the centroid, the point count, the size, and the mean and maximum distance.

With 'Find holes' on, the output also has the fields 'change_inward' and 'change_type'. 'change_inward' has the same sign on every wall: positive = material added, negative = material removed. A hole point shows -10 cm. 'change_type' is 0 (no change), 1 (added), 2 (removed), 3 (hole) or 4 (unmatched). Each site in the '.clusters.json' file has a 'type'. A hole site has a size, an area and, when the projection radius is known, the corrected size. An unmatched site is a patch without a distance that is not empty, for example a box or a person that moved between the scans. Its points have no value in 'change_inward'.
Stage 6: Classify.What to expect:
The run report shows how many points were flagged, as a percentage. 0 % usually means that the threshold is too high. A value near 100 % usually means that it is too low. With clustering on, the report also shows how many damage sites it found, how many flagged points it rejected as isolated noise, and the rejected sites of each limit.

Threshold: 'Load RMS & Suggest Threshold' reads the RMS that Stage 3 saved for the comparison file. Use the same file as in Stage 5, not the M3C2 result. Classify multiplies the RMS by the multiplier. This works only if Stage 3 ran with an alignment. 'Check Threshold Against the Diff File...' reads the distances of the M3C2 file. It shows how many points your threshold flags and how many a bell curve would flag. A multiple of the RMS is correct only when the distances follow a bell curve. With a heavy tail (a quiet middle, but many points far from zero), it flags too many points, and they join into very large sites. The check warns you and suggests a threshold from the spread of the distances.

If no damage site stays after clustering, lower the cluster density or the minimum site size, or raise the gap tolerance (DBSCAN only). On a SLAM map, a smooth offset between the scans can make false sites and hide real damage. Use 'Remove the smooth background' and the size and shape limits for this.
Stage 6: Classify.Next steps: Use the output as the input of Stage 7 (Surface). Open the output in CloudCompare and colour it by 'classified' or 'cluster_id' to see which points were flagged and which damage site they belong to. If necessary, change the settings and run again. If you used 'Find holes', keep 'change_inward' ticked in the 'Carry fields' list of Stage 7 (it is ticked by default). Stage 8 then colours the mesh by change_inward: red where material was added, blue where it was removed, and for a hole.

Stage 7: Surface.Purpose: Makes a triangle mesh from a point cloud, usually the classified change cloud of Stage 6. A mesh is easier to read than points in Omniverse, and it gives surface areas for the flagged damage. Stage 7 runs blender_surface.py in Blender, with the Geometry Nodes recipe in configs\ExtraDownsampling.blend.
Stage 7: Surface.Inputs:
- Classified change cloud .ply ('Choose from project...' in project mode).
- Output mesh .ply (fills in project mode).
- Voxel size.
- Carry fields: a list of the fields of the input .ply. Each ticked field is copied from the nearest input point to each mesh vertex.
- Advanced: Blender program (blender.exe), Blender script, .blend file (recipe) and object name, volume radius, delete further, island filter size, and 'Only this change type'.
- The recipe values are the values saved in ExtraDownsampling.blend. A blank field keeps the value that is in the .blend file.
Stage 7: Surface.Outputs: A triangle mesh .ply with the carried fields. Each carried field is written as a decimal number with the same value (a cluster_id of 3 is written as 3.0). In project mode, the result is recorded on the surface stage of the selected diff, with the values and the carried fields that the run used.
Stage 7: Surface.What to expect:
The recipe first removes each point that has no neighbour nearer than 'Delete further'. Then it makes a volume around the remaining points (voxel size, volume radius) and makes the surface of that volume. The app puts the input points into the recipe object, runs the modifier one time, and saves the result. The app does not change the .blend file. The Terminal tab shows the values that Blender used, the vertex and face counts, and the surface area. A large cloud needs much time and memory.

If the result has no faces, the stage fails. Decrease the voxel size, increase the volume radius, or increase 'Delete further'. The surface is closed around the points, so a single wall becomes a thin closed shell. To change the recipe, edit the .blend file in Blender 5.2 or newer and save it. If your .blend file does not have the inputs of the page, clear the fields.

Carry fields: the default fields are change_type, change_inward, scalar_M3C2_distance and cluster_id, when the input has them. Normals and colours are not in the list, because Blender cannot carry them. Each extra field adds a little time.

Island filter: after the recipe makes the surface, it deletes each separate piece of the mesh that has fewer vertices than the island filter size. These pieces are small bubbles around stray points near the walls. A piece that touches a damage site (an input point with cluster_id 0 or more) is always kept. If the input has no cluster_id field, the recipe cannot see the damage sites. It then deletes every small piece, and the report gives a WARNING. Set the value to 1 to keep every piece.

Only this change type: use it to make a separate surface of one type, for example 4 (unmatched). The carried fields still come from all input points, so a vertex at the edge can show a different change_type. Added and removed points are often scattered, so a surface of one of these types can be many small pieces.
Stage 7: Surface.Next steps: Open the mesh in CloudCompare or Omniverse and check it. Then use it as the Change-highlight input of Stage 8 (Export).

Stage 8: Export to USD.Purpose: Makes one USD scene from the files of the earlier stages, for example for Omniverse. It can also make a .usdz package for web, AR and mobile viewers. Each file that you select becomes one layer of the scene. The baseline and change layers can each be a point cloud or a mesh.
Stage 8: Export to USD.Inputs:
- Baseline .ply or mesh (required). In project mode, it fills from the Cleanup output of the baseline of the project. The environment layer is the same for each diff.
- Change layer .ply or mesh (required). In project mode, it fills from the Stage 7 (Surface) output of the selected diff. The file must have the field change_inward or the M3C2 distance.
- Optional: flagged points, a Stage 6 output. In project mode, the app fills it when Classify ran with 'Keep all points'.
- Optional: damage sites, the .clusters.json file that Stage 6 saves next to its output. In project mode, the app fills it from the Classify output of the diff.
- Optional: damage detail .ply. Make it with the box 'Make the damage detail file'. The button in the box fills the field.
- Output .usd.
- Advanced: the export script, surface labels (a Stage 4 output of the reference scan, used only with damage sites), .usdz package, and downsampling of the point cloud layers.
- The list 'Scene layers' shows what the scene will have.
Stage 8: Export to USD.Outputs:
A .usd scene with these layers under /World/Compartment:
- Baseline: the room, in muted grey.
- ChangeHighlight: the change, in a blue-white-red colour map from the M3C2 distance (or from the carried field of the mesh).
- DamageDetail (optional): the real points of the new scan at the damage, coloured by change type. ChangeHighlight shows the size of the change at the baseline positions, and not the real current shape. DamageDetail shows the current shape.
- FlaggedPoints (optional): only the flagged points, coloured like ChangeHighlight. Hide ChangeHighlight to see only the damage.
- DamageSites (optional): one see-through box for each damage site (Site_00, Site_01 and so on), at the centre of the site and with its size. The colour goes from pale orange to red, and the site with the largest change is red. With surface labels, each site also shows its surface, for example 'Site 03 - wall_2'.
The scene is in metres (metersPerUnit = 1), with Z up and /World as the default prim. With the .usdz option, the app also writes a .usdz package next to the .usd file.
Stage 8: Export to USD.What to expect:
Stage 8 needs 'pip install usd-core plyfile' in addition to the other packages. It accepts point clouds and meshes.

If walls block the view in Omniverse, move the near-clip distance of the camera, or hide Baseline in the Stage panel.

Downsampling: it affects only the point cloud layers. It keeps one point for each voxel cell and removes near-duplicate points from overlapping scan passes. It does not remove real detail if the voxel size is smaller than the smallest feature that you want to see.

Damage detail: 'Extract Damage Detail...' runs extract_damage_detail.py. It uses the same running lock and Stop button as a stage run. The Radius field shows the normal scale of Stage 5 when the value is known. In project mode, the result goes into the export folder of the diff, and the field 'Damage detail .ply' shows it. The Classify output gives the places of the damage. The script takes the points of the new scan that are near these places, and gives each point the change type of the nearest place. If the Classify file has change_inward, the script uses it before scalar_M3C2_distance. With a 'Keep all points' output, the script uses only the flagged points.

Damage sites: select a Site_NN prim in the Stage panel of Omniverse. The Property panel shows its values under 'Raw USD Properties': delta:pointCount, delta:meanMagnitude and delta:maxMagnitude (metres, without sign), and delta:centroid and delta:extent (metres). The DamageSites group shows the Classify counts: delta:nFlagged, delta:nConfirmed and delta:nNoise. A flat site (for example a dent in one wall) gets a box of at least 2 cm in each direction, so that you can see it. With surface labels, delta:surface is the surface that most points of the site are on, and delta:surfaceShare (0 to 1) is the part of the points on that surface. A low value shows a site on more than one surface, for example in a corner. If the file is not a cluster summary, the export stops with an error and does not write a .usd file.

Typed damage sites: when the damage sites file comes from a Stage 6 run with 'Find holes', each site has a type. The colour shows the type: added = pale orange to red, removed = blue, hole = purple, unmatched = teal. The prim name shows the type, for example 'Site 03 (hole)'. Each typed site has delta:type and delta:meanChangeInward. A hole site also has delta:width, delta:height, delta:thickness, delta:area, delta:ringValidFraction, delta:fillFraction and the corrected values. The DamageSites group has delta:nHoles and delta:nHolePoints.
Stage 8: Export to USD.Next steps: Open the .usd file in Omniverse or in another USD viewer, or the .usdz file in a web, AR or mobile viewer. Check that the baseline is muted grey and that the change regions are coloured by size. If you used DamageDetail, check that it shows the real current shape.
